turns.user_message: I have a systemd service for our internal collector. After a config change, `sudo systemctl start collector` returns 'Failed to start collector.service: Unit collector.service has failed.' and `systemctl status` shows it as failed. Logs aren't obvious to me. What's the right diagnostic order?
turns.se_response_summary: systemd hides the actual error in journal; status is just summary. Order: (1) systemctl status <unit> — exit code, last 10 journal entries; (2) journalctl -u <unit> -e — full unit log with binary's actual error; (3) systemd-analyze verify <unit> — catches malformed unit files. Status-code table: 203/EXEC=binary missing/non-exec; 200/USER=user not found; start-limit-hit=StartLimitBurst exhausted (do reset-failed before next start).
hints: Where does the actual error live (not in `status` summary)?
After many fast restarts, what does systemd do, and what command resets it?

turns.user_message: status shows: Active: failed (Result: start-limit-hit), Process: ExecStart=... (code=exited, status=2). Journal shows: 'Error parsing config: yaml: unmarshal error at line 14: cannot unmarshal !!str into int', then 'collector.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=2/INVALIDARGUMENT', then 'start request repeated too quickly'.
turns.se_response_summary: Two issues stacked: (1) Real cause = YAML parse error at line 14 (string where int expected, e.g. timeout: "30" not timeout: 30). Open file, fix the type. (2) Compound issue = start-limit-hit. systemd refuses further attempts even after fix. Path: fix YAML → sudo systemctl reset-failed collector → sudo systemctl start collector. Validate: journalctl -u collector -f shows clean startup.
hints: What two distinct issues does the journal output show?
After fixing the underlying issue, what's the one-time command needed to reset the start-limit counter?

turns.user_message: Yep — line 14 was `timeout: "30"` instead of `timeout: 30`. Fixed and started clean. To prevent the start-limit issue, what's the right tuning?
turns.se_response_summary: Two-part: loosen StartLimit + validate config before starting. (A) [Unit] StartLimitIntervalSec=600s StartLimitBurst=10; [Service] Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5s. 10 restarts in 10min = catches truly broken without locking out for transient. daemon-reload after editing. (B) [Service] ExecStartPre=/usr/local/bin/collector --config-check /etc/collector.yaml. Bad config now fails the start with a clear message before main process tries.
hints: What's the [Unit]-level setting that controls how aggressive the restart-loop guard is?
How do you catch a bad config before the main process even tries?

turns.user_message: Different unit problem: I have a `mounts/data.mount` unit that's been failing since the upstream NFS server hiccuped. NFS is back but the unit is still failed and won't auto-recover. How does that work?
turns.se_response_summary: Mount units are weirder than service units; don't auto-restart the same way. Path: (1) sudo systemctl reset-failed mounts-data.mount; sudo systemctl start mounts-data.mount. (2) For NFS, fstab options should include _netdev,soft,timeo=30,retrans=3 so hangs are recoverable. (3) For auto-recovery, drop a systemd timer that watchdog-restarts the failed mount. (4) mount units in newer systemd (>=v244) DO support Restart=on-failure.
hints: Why don't mount units auto-recover the same way as service units?
What fstab options make NFS mounts recover from hangs gracefully?
